title: The wandering mind
hookLine: a 2010 Harvard study found minds wander nearly half the time, and wandering tracked lower mood (Killingsworth and Gilbert)

lines: THE LAST TEN MINUTES OF ROAD.
cards: You get to the bottom of a page and realize you have no idea what it said. Your eyes did the work. You were somewhere else: an argument from last week, what to make for dinner, a trip you haven't booked.
Or you drive home and can't remember the last ten minutes of road. What wasn't known, until fairly recently, was how often this happens in an ordinary day, and whether it matters for how we feel.
Two researchers used a phone to find out.

teach.h: AN APP THAT PINGED AT RANDOM.
teach.b: In 2010, Matthew Killingsworth and Daniel Gilbert, psychologists at Harvard, published a study in the journal Science.
They built an iPhone app that pinged people at random moments during their day and asked three quick questions. How are you feeling right now? What are you doing right now?
Are you thinking about something other than what you're doing? About two thousand two hundred fifty adults took part, giving a quarter of a million answers.
The first finding: minds were wandering in nearly half of the samples, about forty-seven percent, and in every activity but one, at least thirty percent of the time.
The second: people were less happy when their minds were wandering than when they weren't. Even wandering to pleasant topics didn't make them happier than staying with what they were doing.
Their title put it bluntly: a wandering mind is an unhappy mind. Now yesterday's three questions. Who was studied?
People with iPhones who chose to sign up for a happiness app, so not everyone on earth. How many? A lot, which is a strength.
Compared to what? Each person's wandering moments against their own focused moments. But it's not an experiment; nobody was told to wander.

So the arrow could run both ways: a low mood might send the mind wandering. The authors looked at timing and found wandering tended to come before the dip more than after, which is suggestive, not final.

teach.h: WHO, HOW MANY, COMPARED TO WHAT.
teach.b: Many of the contemplative traditions on this path train attention.
This study doesn't prove them right. It does suggest the problem they were working on is real, and common.

how: Attention practices in several traditions work by noticing when the mind has wandered and gently returning it; researchers study wandering by sampling people's experience at random moments.

games.q: you're designing a study of everyday minds. how do Killingsworth and Gilbert catch thoughts as they happen?
games.why: an iPhone app pinged about 2,250 adults at random moments, collecting a quarter of a million answers.

practice: Rest your attention on your breath, and sooner or later you'll find you've drifted; that moment of noticing is the whole practice.
When it comes, ask silently where it is now, name where it went, planning, remembering, worrying, and gently come back to the breath. Catch it once, then catch it again.

wordCard.voice: Killingsworth, co-author of the 2010 study where minds wandered nearly half the time, and wandering tracked lower mood.

carryVoice: Your line: where is it now. Noticing the drift is where coming back begins. See you tomorrow.
